memory_line: Hypertensive emergency: lower it, don't drop it.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 3:00 AM. He's 69.
• BP (blood pressure) 228/126, pounding headache, blurry vision
• PRN (as-needed) order: IV (intravenous) labetalol

❌ 3 mistakes
1️⃣ Pushed dose after dose, chasing 120/80
2️⃣ No BP or neuro checks between doses
3️⃣ Never called for a target or a higher level of care
➡️ 3:50 AM: BP 102/58, slurred speech, left arm weak. Rapid response.

🧮 The math
• 25% of 228 is 57
• First-hour floor: a systolic around 171, not 120

🩺 Hypertensive emergency (LOWER, DON'T DROP)
• Very high BP plus signs of organ damage: chest pain, confusion, vision changes, shortness of breath, little urine
• The brain gets used to high pressure. Drop it fast and blood flow to the brain falls: stroke risk
• Very high BP (over 180/120) with NO new organ damage is now called severe hypertension (the old name was urgency): oral meds, no rapid lowering

✅ The right move
• Call now. ICU-level care, IV drip as ordered
• First hour: down no more than 25%
• Then under 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then a systolic of 130 to 140 over the next 24 to 48 hours
• BP every 5 to 15 minutes, neuro checks
• Exceptions, like aortic dissection, follow their own targets, as ordered

🧠 Hypertensive emergency: lower it, don't drop it.
share_line: 📤 Send this to the nurse who'd chase 120/80 at 3 AM.
sources: 2025 AHA/ACC (American Heart Association, American College of Cardiology) Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults, Section 6.2: Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension
rn_checks: Hypertensive emergency: severe BP elevation (often over 180/120) with new or worsening target organ damage
Targets (2025 AHA/ACC, Section 6.2): first hour SBP down no more than 25%; next 2 to 6 hours under 160/100; next 24 to 48 hours cautiously to SBP 130 to 140; ICU admission
Compelling conditions have faster first-hour targets (SBP under 140 for most, under 120 for aortic dissection), as ordered; 2025 no longer lists pheochromocytoma
Story: repeated IV labetalol pushes, BP 228/126 to 102/58 in under an hour, then stroke signs. Realistic?
